title: Recording for Victor and choosing tunes by audience response
summary: RCA let him record whatever he wanted and he picked tunes by what audiences requested.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And, you began recording for Victor around '38 was it?
Somewhere around then. I believe it was '38, '37 or '38.
And you stayed with them when, until about 1950?
Right. Yeah, we had some good years together down there.
I used to follow either follow each other like Pats Waller was using, was in the same studio a lot. Tommy Dorsey was in the same studio a lot. You know, follow each other one way or the other.

I used to go down there like when we played the Paramount or the Strand. We'd finish the show at 11:00. We was down there recording at 1:00 at night. And, they practically let me record practically anything I want.

Yeah. Well, you had a very popular sound at that time. I mean, it had come together and, you know, with the people. It was just a very popular thing not only at the Savoy, but just about every place else that you were playing.
I used to have 4 and 5 records on a lot vendors at the same time.

That's how RCA let me do it. I used to take my whole book down there. And, they didn't tell me what to record. They'd just say what's your next number? I'd say, 'Get in there and get 495 out.' I called all my tunes by numbers.

And then, I used to judge my recordings by how the people received me, the tune that I was playing where the place I played - a dance or a theater. I said if they started requesting the tunes over and over, that would be the tune I would record on my next session. You know, that's how I used to pick my tunes out, you know, according to the public.
